You can also read Drew over at SFGATE, and buy Drew’s books while you’re at it. I’m on my hands and knees, working in the backyard. I rarely engage in any sort of gardening work, and by “rarely,” I mean never. I still have bitter memories of being forced to do yard work at my parents’ house as a kid, grabbing at the little weeds sprouting out of the cracks in the front walk, feeling the sweat gush out of me as I yanked and pulled and twisted. Every weed I uprooted just made me think about the countless more I still had to deal with. I knew many people who adored tending to their land, my mother included, but I was not among them. All I ever wanted to do was go back inside and watch MTV. The only satisfaction I got from doing the job was when parents paid me after the fact. Even then, they’d still point out all of the weeds I’d missed. Gardening was a hobby for the sadistic, I believed. Three back surgeries later, I had an all-too-convenient out to save myself from every getting my hands dirty again. My wife and I now have a nice-sized yard that requires care, and for the past 20 years, that work has been handled either by landscaping pros, my green-thumbed mother-in-law—who would often come by our house unannounced just to garden—or my wife. I myself never bothered going out there. After all, I had a bad back: a legitimate alibi that men like me love nothing more than to abuse. I used to mow our law myself right after we moved in 20 years ago, but with only a push mower at our disposal, I quickly deemed that job far too taxing.

Best of all, Journelly keeps its data as an Org file so I can query or edit it in Emacs. Of course, Journelly has a search function but sometimes I want to do a more complicated search or even to just count the number of entries in the database (4361 as of right now). Having the database as an Org file means that my data is available on all my devices, even if that device is a Mac.
I’ve been using Journelly since March 2025, ever since it was in beta, and have never looked back. Lately, however, it’s been getting a bit laggy, something I put down to my large database. I was on the verge of truncating my active data to the most recent entries in order to improve performance when Álvaro Ramírez pushed a new beta—v1.5(4)—that completely solved the problem. Now Journelly performs just like it did when I started.
If you are an Emacs user and are using an iPhone/iPad, I can’t think of any reason why you wouldn’t want to use Journelly. It allows you to integrate your day-to-day note taking with the power of Org mode. Even if you aren’t an Emacs user, you’ll probably find Journelly useful. It can also save its data as a markdown file so you can still get all the benefits of an easily accessible and editable database even if you prefer another editor.

entry.title: Randy Ridenour: Emacs Literate Calc Mode
entry.summary:
Soulver on the Mac.
I recently stumbled on Literate Calc Mode by Robin1 that does everything I was using Soulver for, and I now have one more reason to not leave Emacs. It’s in Melpa, so installing it is simple. Once required, it provides both literate-calc-mode and literate-calc-minor-mode. I find the minor mode particularly useful for Org mode scratch buffers. For example, I used it recently to sketch out some details for a conference funding request. In an Org buffer, I entered:
Expenses for February 2027 Baylor Trip
Hotel = 500 Parking = 10 Registration = 295 Mileage = 300 Meals = 200
Total = Hotel + Parking + Registration + Mileage + Meals
M-x literate-calc-minor-mode instantly changed it to this:
Expenses for February 2027 Baylor Trip
Hotel = 500 => Hotel: 500 Parking = 10 => Parking: 10 Registration = 295 => Registration: 295 Mileage = 300 => Mileage: 300 Meals = 200 => Meals: 200
Total = Hotel + Parking + Registration + Mileage + Meals => Total: 1,305
=> is not editable and displayed in a lighter shade. Changing one of the variable values results in an instant update of the total. It uses Calc, so it is able to do almost anything that Calc can do. So far, I’ve used it to plan travel expenses and to build material lists for woodworking projects. It works flawlessly and I’ve found it surprisingly useful to have a scratchpad that can automatically do the math.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Announcing mdired, or adding a chainsaw to Dired
entry.summary: The ability to mark items in GNU Emacs Dired allows for bulk operations on both files and directories. With marking, onerous tasks can be turned into a trivial ones. While default Dired has many bulk operation commands, not everything is covered. That is the motivation for mdired, an Elisp package which extends Dired with some SIMD-style commands. Using these commands fall into two steps: Mark the items of interest in Dired. Run the mdired command. mdired supports the following four commands: mdired-copy: copy a single file to multiple directories. mdired-do-command: run an Elisp command or named keyboard macro on multiple files. mdired-compile: run compile on multiple directories. mdired-byte-recompile: byte-compile selected files or directories. Refer to the mdired User Guide for more details on usage. Closing Thoughts Bulk operation commands are chainsaws. Use them with caution. That said, they are great for improvised workflows: “Here’s this file that I want copied to a bunch of directories.” “I want to do the same edit operation on this set of files. I’ve got a named keyboard macro ready to go on them.” “I want to run the same make command on a bunch of directories.” As mdired is new, I’m open to feedback on it. entry.title: Raymond Zeitler: Highlight Active Emacs Window
entry.summary:
https://emacs.stackexchange.com/a/36240/47342, CodyChan provides a few options "to better distinguish between focused window." But the one I like best is highlight-selected-window, which, rather than highlighting the selected window, changes the background color of all the unselected windows. The effect is that the active window stands out in comparison to the others.
The especially neat thing about this solution is that when the minibuffer is active, the background of all the windows is altered. So it's obvious even when Emacs is expecting input -- something I often miss.
I've changed the color of the buffer-face-set background from "#111" (sienna4) to "antiquewhite2" because I still need to read the content of inactive windows. The original color is too dark.
flash-active-buffer, which sets the background color of the active window temporarily. I changed the color to palegreen just because. I use s-? as a keybinding. It's a bit awkward, but it's as if I use "?" to ask, "Where am I?" The function highlight-selected-window works so well that I don't think I'll need flash-active-buffer.
The color names that Emacs understands are stored in color-name-rgb-alist.

entry.title: Irreal: Emacs Turns 50
entry.summary:
MIT Technology Review there’s a nice article on Emacs turning 50 this year. It gives a short history of Emacs starting from its TECO days. Most of that history is pretty well known to seasoned Emacs users but it’s still interesting.
What the article doesn’t give is the exact day of Emacs’ 50th birthday. That’s not surprising. The early history of Emacs involved the researchers at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory agreeing on a standard set of TECO macros in order to improve collaboration. That was undoubtedly an ongoing process that didn’t have a well defined beginning or end so it’s easy to understand why the exact birthday of Emacs is a little murky.
Regardless, we can all celebrate Emacs’ 50th year. It’s remarkable when you think about it. Very few programs last that long. There’s FORTRAN and Lisp, of course, but I can’t think of any other piece of software with that sort of longevity. There is, to be sure, a Ship of Theseus aspect to that longevity but it’s one shared by FORTRAN and Lisp as well.
Who knows what things will look like in another 50 years but if we still have editors, I’m putting my money on Emacs still being around. Wouldn’t that be something?

entry.title: Irreal: Electric Quote Mode
entry.summary:
Unicode punctuation in Emacs. His post is mainly concerned with the vagaries of dealing with English and Polish punctuation in the same document but a lot of the heavy lifting is accomplished with Electric Quote Mode.
The main problem is handling single and double quotes ‘like this’ and “like this”. Because I do almost all my writing in Org mode, I use the ':t option to turn the ASCII double quote (") into their curved typeset equivalents on export. That’s supposed to do the same with single quotes but I could never get it to work for me and always had to add then manually.
Fortunately, it’s easy to make everything work right in the buffer as you type. You merely turn electric-quote-mode on and it takes care of everything for you. By default it acts the way TeX used to by requiring “ for an opening double quote and ” for the closing double quote and similarly for single quotes. You can make it accept ” and ‘ instead by setting electric-quote-replace-double and electric-quote-context-sensitive to t.
Electric Quote Mode is global so turning it on enables it for all your buffers. You can use electric-quote-local-mode if you want it only in the current buffer. You can toggle either of them on or off by simply calling Meta+x electric-quote....
If you have to deal different quote notation for two or more languages, take a look at mbork’s post for a nifty solution.

entry.title: Irreal: Controlling Where Isearch Starts Searching
entry.summary:
new Emacs trick from Emacs Dwelling. Well, new to me. It turns out it’s been in Emacs since 28.1 so for about four and a half years.
Here’s the problem. When you call isearch it starts searching at the current point location to the bottom of the file. You can cause it to wrap around and continue searching at the top of the file but this isn’t always convenient. As a result, many people always start their search by moving to the top of the buffer first. But this isn’t always convenient either. For example, if you quit the search you go back to the top of the file, not where you started.
Sometimes you want a bit more control: perhaps you want to start at the first match or the last match and if you quit, you’d like to be back where you started. Well this is Emacs so of course you can do that. The nice thing is that it’s already built in. There are no packages to install, you just enable it my setting isearch-allow-motion to t.
You can start the search at any of:
The current point position The first match in the file The last match in the file The first match before the window The first match after the window
